title: Picot — the decorative loop edge
subtitle: Three chains closed back to the first with a slip stitch — a tiny decorative point
excerpt: Picot is three chains closed back into the first chain with a slip stitch. The result is a tiny raised loop — the standard decorative finish for shawl edges, lace borders, baby clothes, and collar edgings.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776 — picot edging in needlework and crochet lace. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Vol. 1 (1886) — the three-chain picot in edging work.

glossaryTerms.definition: Three chains closed into the first chain with a slip stitch to form a small raised loop. Used as a decorative edge finish on shawls, lace, and garments. Abbreviated 'p' in pattern shorthand.

heroPrompt: Close-up of a crochet picot edging in white cotton thread, showing several evenly-spaced picot loops along an edge, delicate and clear against a dark background.

inlineDiagramTopics.description: The three chains made, with the hook about to insert back into the first chain to close

content.text: is the simplest decorative crochet edge — three chains, then a slip stitch back into the first chain to close the loop into a small raised point. Done along the edge of a finished piece, regularly spaced between double crochet or slip stitch anchors, picots create the traditional frilled finish seen on shawls, doilies, and baby garments.
Work a row of double crochet around the finished edge, evenly spaced.
On the picot row: *work 1 dc in each of the next 3 dc from the previous row, then make the picot.
To make the picot: ch 3. Insert hook into the first of the 3 chains just made — that is, the chain furthest from the hook.
Yarn over and pull through both the chain and the loop on the hook — slip stitch complete. The three chains form a small closed loop.
Continue: *1 dc in each of the next 3 sts, picot. Repeat from * to end of edge.

attrs.title: Adjusting picot size
attrs.body: Three chains make a small, tight picot point. Four or five chains make a larger loop with a looser drape — more like a scallop than a point. Match the picot chain count to the scale of the piece: three chains for fine cotton, four or five for DK or aran.

items.symptom: Picots face inward rather than outward
items.cause: Closing the picot into the wrong chain — inserting into the chain nearest the hook instead of the farthest
items.fix: The slip stitch goes into the first chain made, which is the one furthest from the hook. Count three chains back from the hook and insert there.

items.symptom: Picots are uneven — some larger, some smaller
items.cause: Inconsistent chain tension or inconsistent spacing of the anchor dc stitches
items.fix: Work all three chains at the same tension. Use a stitch marker to mark every 3rd anchor dc so the picots land at even intervals.

content.text: Picot chain is a row of picots separated by chain spaces rather than dc anchors — giving a more open, floating border. Both are Victorian-documented finishes that appear across the whole needlework record.
